description: Propp's character types, Todorov's equilibrium arc, and how narrative hooks audiences in.
content_html:
Why Narrative Theory Matters

Stories are among the oldest and most powerful tools in any media producer’s toolkit. Whether you are watching a streaming drama, reading a comic strip, playing a video game or watching a music video with a story thread, you are experiencing a narrative. Media Studies asks you to analyse how narratives are constructed, who they centre, and what that construction tells us about the values and assumptions of the producer. Two theorists are central to this analysis at GCSE level: Vladimir Propp and Tzvetan Todorov.

Vladimir Propp: Character Functions

The Russian folklorist Vladimir Propp analysed a large collection of folk tales in his 1928 work Morphology of the Folktale and found that, despite the variety of stories, the same types of character appeared repeatedly. Propp argued that these character types — which he called character functions — were structurally essential to the narrative: the story could not proceed without each role being filled, though one character could fill more than one role.

The seven character functions Propp identified are: the hero (who undertakes the quest), the villain (who creates the central conflict), the donor (who gives the hero a special gift, skill or object), the helper (who supports the hero), the princess or sought-for person (who is typically the goal or reward of the quest), the dispatcher (who sends the hero on the quest), and the false hero (who appears heroic but is not). At GCSE, you are expected to know and apply these seven types, not Propp’s full list of 31 narrative functions.

Key Fact

Propp’s seven character functions: hero, villain, donor, helper, princess (sought-for person), dispatcher, false hero. One character can fill more than one role. Source: Propp, Morphology of the Folktale (1928).

Propp developed his theory from folk tales, but the functions travel well into modern media. In a typical superhero film, the hero is clearly the protagonist with abilities; the villain creates the central threat; a mentor figure or organisation often acts as both dispatcher and donor (setting the hero on their mission and supplying them with tools or training); a sidekick fills the helper role; and a love interest or protected community represents the princess function. A false hero might be a colleague who seems trustworthy but proves to be compromised.

Propp is also useful for critiquing media products. When a narrative consistently places women only in the princess function (passive, to be rescued) or gives all the active hero and villain roles to men, Propp’s framework gives you precise language to describe this pattern. Conversely, when a media product subverts Propp by making the princess the hero, or by making the donor the villain, you can describe that subversion precisely and explain what meaning it creates. Exam questions sometimes ask you to apply Propp to a media product you have studied, so practise mapping character functions onto at least one television drama and one other narrative media form.

Tzvetan Todorov: Equilibrium and Disruption

The Bulgarian narratologist Tzvetan Todorov argued that most narratives follow a five-stage arc. They begin with an equilibrium — a state of normality or balance at the start of the story. A disruption then breaks that equilibrium, setting the narrative in motion. A period of recognition (the characters acknowledge that something has gone wrong) leads to an attempt to repair the disruption. Finally a new equilibrium is reached — which is not identical to the opening state, because the characters and their world have been changed by events.

This five-stage structure (equilibrium → disruption → recognition → repair → new equilibrium) is sometimes compressed in shorter media forms. A television advertisement for an insurance company might open with a couple contentedly driving (equilibrium), show their car being hit (disruption), and close with them smiling after a smooth insurance claim (new equilibrium). A music video narrative might move through the same arc in three minutes. The structure is useful precisely because it is flexible enough to apply across all narrative media forms.

Key Fact

Todorov’s narrative arc: (1) equilibrium → (2) disruption → (3) recognition → (4) repair → (5) new equilibrium. The new equilibrium is never identical to the opening one — the narrative has changed things.

Enigma and Closure

Both Propp and Todorov help explain the structure of narratives, but neither fully explains why audiences keep watching or reading. Two concepts borrowed from Roland Barthes’s code theory are particularly useful here. The enigma code describes the unresolved questions that a narrative plants early and answers only gradually — the classic “who did it?” of a crime drama, or the ambiguous opening image of a thriller. Audiences engage with narratives partly to resolve enigmas.

Closure is the satisfying resolution of those enigmas — the detective names the murderer, the hero defeats the villain, the couple reunite. Closed narratives (those that resolve all their threads) are associated with mainstream entertainment. Open narratives (those that deliberately leave questions unanswered) are associated with art-house or prestige media. A streaming drama might use a cliff-hanger ending to deny closure deliberately and compel audiences to watch the next episode — a commercial use of the enigma code to drive continued engagement.

Todorov’s arc assumes a linear narrative — one that moves chronologically from beginning to end. Many mainstream media products do follow this structure because it is the most immediately accessible for audiences. However, non-linear narratives deliberately disrupt chronological order, using flashbacks, flash-forwards or multiple perspectives to create different effects: mystery (we see the aftermath before the cause), empathy (a flashback gives us a character’s backstory before a key decision), or complexity (simultaneous storylines that converge).

Non-linear narratives are common in prestige television, literary fiction adaptations and video games, where the audience’s active role in exploring the narrative is part of the experience. For Media Studies analysis, identifying whether a narrative is linear or non-linear is the first step — the more interesting question is always: what effect does that structural choice have on how audiences engage with the product?
exam_tip_html: When applying Propp or Todorov to a media product in the exam, avoid summarising the theory and then separately summarising the product — this is the most common reason students miss the higher marks. Instead, apply the theory directly to a specific moment: ‘At the opening of the episode, Todorov’s equilibrium is established through…’ or ‘The mentor figure acts as Propp’s donor by…’. One theorist applied precisely to two or three specific moments is worth more than both theorists mentioned vaguely. Never confuse Propp (character functions in folk tales, 1928) with Todorov (equilibrium arc) — they are different theorists with different arguments.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Vladimir Propp (Morphology of the Folktale, 1928) identified seven recurring character functions: hero, villain, donor, helper, princess, dispatcher, false hero. One character can fill more than one role.
  • Tzvetan Todorov argued most narratives follow a five-stage arc: equilibrium → disruption → recognition → repair → new equilibrium. The new equilibrium differs from the opening state.
  • The enigma code (unresolved questions) pulls audiences through a narrative; closure (resolution of all questions) provides the satisfying ending. Producers use these tools deliberately to generate and sustain audience engagement.

practice_questions.text:
In Propp's theory, which character function describes the figure who sends the hero on the quest?
A. Helper
B. Donor
C. Dispatcher
D. False hero
practice_questions.marks: C — Dispatcher. Do not accept A (helper supports the hero but does not initiate the quest), B (donor provides a gift or skill), or D (false hero appears heroic but is not).

practice_questions.text: Identify the stage in Todorov's narrative arc that immediately follows the disruption.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for 'recognition' (the characters acknowledge that something has gone wrong). Do not accept 'repair' (this is the stage after recognition) or 'new equilibrium'.

practice_questions.text: Identify one example of the enigma code in a media product you have studied and explain how it engages the audience.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for clearly identifying a specific unresolved question or puzzle in a named media product. 1 further mark for explaining how this enigma creates suspense or compels the audience to continue watching, reading or playing.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Todorov's narrative theory can be used to analyse the structure of a media product.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: names Todorov and/or describes one stage of the arc (1 mark). Developing: accurately describes the five-stage arc and attempts to apply it to a named product (2 marks). Secure/Mastering: clearly applies at least three stages of the arc to specific moments in a named product and explains how the structure shapes the audience's engagement (3 marks).

practice_questions.text: Explain how Propp's character functions can be used to analyse a media product you have studied, and what this analysis reveals about the values encoded in that product.
practice_questions.marks: Emerging: identifies one or two character functions with limited application (1 mark). Developing: maps two or three functions onto characters in a named product (2 marks). Secure: accurately maps multiple functions and begins to comment on what the distribution of active and passive roles reveals about the product's values (3 marks). Mastering: sophisticated application of Propp's functions to a named product, with analysis of which character types dominate, which are absent or subverted, and what this encodes about gender, power or ideology (4 marks).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how narrative theory (including at least one named theorist) can be applied to a media product you have studied to explain how it engages its audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Emerging (1-2): brief description of narrative structure or named theorist with little or no application to a specific product.
Developing (3-4): applies one theoretical framework (Propp or Todorov) to a named product with some accuracy; may only describe without fully explaining the audience engagement effect.
Secure (5): sustained and accurate application of at least one named theorist (Propp or Todorov) to specific moments in a named product; explains clearly how narrative structure generates engagement (enigma, closure, character identification).
Mastering (6): sophisticated analysis using at least one theorist applied precisely to the named product; integrates enigma and closure into the argument; may compare linear and non-linear choices or consider how the structure was subverted; precise and fluent use of terminology throughout.

knowledge_checks.q: In which year did Vladimir Propp publish Morphology of the Folktale?
In Todorov's narrative theory, what is the 'new equilibrium'?
options: The moment the disruption first occurs
The original state of normality at the beginning of the story
The state of balance reached at the end, after the disruption has been resolved
The moment when the hero defeats the villain

knowledge_checks.q: In Propp's theory, the _____ is the character who gives the hero a magical agent, useful skill or special object.
An unresolved question built into a narrative that pulls the audience forward is called the _____ code.
Match each narrative concept to its correct description.
right: The satisfying resolution of all narrative questions and tensions
The event that breaks the opening state of normality
The stable, ordered state at the start of a story

flashcard_questions.q: What work is Vladimir Propp famous for in narrative theory?
How many character functions did Propp identify at GCSE level?
flashcard_questions.a: Seven: hero, villain, donor, helper, princess, dispatcher, false hero.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Propp's 'donor' character function do?
flashcard_questions.a: Gives the hero a magical agent, useful skill or special object to aid the quest.
Appears heroic but proves to be untrustworthy or not the true protagonist.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the first stage of Todorov's narrative arc?
flashcard_questions.a: Equilibrium — the stable, ordered state before anything goes wrong.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the final stage of Todorov's narrative arc?
flashcard_questions.a: New equilibrium — a restored balance that differs from the opening state.
A narrative that moves forward in strict chronological order from beginning to end.

flashcard_questions.q: What is closure in narrative theory?
flashcard_questions.a: The satisfying resolution of all narrative questions and tensions at the end.
An unresolved question built into a narrative that compels the audience to keep watching or reading.

flashcard_questions.q: In Propp's theory, which character sends the hero on the quest?

glossary_terms.definition: The organised sequence of events in a media product that creates meaning and generates audience engagement.
The seven character roles that Vladimir Propp identified as recurring across folk tales and many media narratives.
In Propp's theory, the character who undertakes the quest and drives the narrative forward.
In Propp's theory, the character who opposes the hero and creates conflict.
In Propp's theory, the character who gives the hero a magical agent or useful skill to help the quest.
In Propp's theory, the character who assists or supports the hero.
In Todorov's narrative theory, the stable, ordered state at the beginning of a story before anything goes wrong.
In Todorov's narrative theory, the event or action that breaks the opening equilibrium and sets the narrative in motion.
In Todorov's narrative theory, the new state of balance reached at the end of the narrative after the disruption has been resolved.
An unresolved question or puzzle built into a narrative that pulls the audience forward, wanting to know what will happen next.
The satisfying resolution of all narrative questions and tensions at the end of a media product.
A narrative that moves forward in a single, chronological direction from beginning to end.
A narrative that does not follow strict chronological order, using techniques such as flashbacks, flash-forwards or multiple perspectives.
